html:
A trade treaty between Britain and Siam, signed in Bangkok in April 1855, that opened the kingdom to free trade.

King Mongkut had watched Britain force open China in the Opium War. When John Bowring, the governor of Hong Kong, arrived to negotiate, Mongkut chose to give way rather than fight. The treaty:

  • capped import duties at 3 percent,
  • ended the royal monopolies on foreign trade,
  • let British subjects trade freely, live in Bangkok and buy land near it,
  • put British subjects under their own consul's courts, not Siamese ones,
  • allowed rice to be exported.

Similar treaties with the United States, France and other powers soon followed. Siam lost control of its tariffs and its courts over foreigners, much as China and Japan did under their unequal treaties.

The economic effect was large. Farmers cleared the Chao Phraya delta for rice, and rice became Siam's main export for a century. The treaty also bought time: by meeting Western demands without war, Mongkut and his son Chulalongkorn kept the kingdom free.
sum: A trade treaty between Britain and Siam, signed in Bangkok in April 1855, that opened the kingdom to free trade.
